The Lead

The bottom is falling twice as fast as the top.

Start with the number nobody prints on a yard sign. In ZIP 33907 — mid-Fort Myers, McGregor to US-41 — Zillow's typical-value index for starter-tier homes is down 31.6% from its 2022 peak. The same index, top tier, same streets, same hurricanes: down 17.7%. One ZIP code holding two different housing markets, and the cheaper one is falling nearly twice as fast. That gap is the story of July, and of the three years behind it.

The papers spent the month telling two stories that sound like a contradiction: luxury is “spreading across Southwest Florida,” and home construction is “slowing dramatically.” The ledger reconciles them in one line: nothing is spreading. Everything is repricing down — the top tier is simply falling least, so it stands taller as the water drops around it. In every Lee and Collier ZIP where Zillow publishes tier data, both tiers are down year over year by May's index, and the bottom falls at twice the rate or worse. 33907: −13.9% against the top's −7.1%. 33919: −13.2% against −7.0%. And in 34105 the starter tier falls six times as fast: −9.5% against −1.5%. In Old Naples, 34102, the spread between the two tiers now computes to 11.2x — $5.33M over $473,850, one ZIP.

Why does the top hold? Cash. Sixty-one percent of Naples closings in May were all-cash by NABOR's count; the national figure for June was 25% by NAR's. A market where three of every five buyers never call a lender is a market where the 30-year rate is somebody else's problem. And here is the detail that kills the easy explanation: money is cheaper than it was a year ago — 6.58% against 6.74% — and the entry tier kept falling anyway. It was never just rates.

Underneath it, Florida tax law quietly holds the sellers hostage. The Save Our Homes cap shields a median 36.71% of home value from taxation across 192,973 homesteaded Lee County parcels. Sell into a falling market and that shield resets to zero at the next house. So owners sit: qualified sales ran 64.2 per 1,000 parcels in 2025 — a full standard deviation (z −1.08) under their own three-year norm. Owners who can't afford to leave, buyers who won't reach the ask, and prices grinding down in the space between them.

A record print did land: a $4,425,000 median for single-family sales inside Naples city limits in May, up 66.2% year over year — on all of forty sales (Redfin, city grain). Read it as mix, not momentum. Forty transactions of whatever is still trading, in the one tier still trading. The top's resilience is real. Its headlines are noisier than it is.

[Inference]  Our call, preregistered in the ledger at the bottom of this issue: the tier gap holds or widens through the summer prints. The number that would prove us wrong is written down there, in a form you can check.

What the papers said · What the ledger says

“Coldest market in America,” says the warmest tier in Florida.

On 07/23/2026 the Fort Myers paper ran “A year later, SW Florida still among America's coldest housing markets.” Three days before that: “In the worst state, Southwest Florida foreclosures highest in America.” National-list framing, local dateline — the coldest-market story is a franchise now, and July was its anniversary issue. The ledger's verdict: cold is real. Uniform cold is false.

Realtor.com's own June table says both at once. Over three years, Lee County's median sold price is down 11.25% while the state of Florida is dead flat (−0.13%) — Lee County genuinely is the state's downside outlier. But thirty minutes south, Naples is off 1.57% over the same three years. Barely a scratch. If Southwest Florida is among America's coldest markets, somebody forgot to tell the tier that pays cash.

The genre's other staple — the record print — is cut from one cloth, coast to coast: Palm Beach's May median landed at $15.8M on thirteen sales; Miami Beach $7.1M on twenty-six; Naples $4.425M on forty; Sarasota $710K on forty-nine — while Boca Raton, the one mid-market city in the set, sat flat on ninety-four. Every ultra-luxury core in Florida prints a giant thin-sample number; the normal market doesn't. The genre reads mix as momentum — in both directions.

And when a “cold market” headline collides with a “tightening market” stat, check the clocks. They are set to different years:

Our market-heat reading is 64 of 100 and tightening — measured against last year: active inventory −17.7%, days-on-market shrinking. Our seller-stress reading is 63 of 100 and rising — measured against 2019–21: 18.7% of listings get delisted, and by Realtor.com's June measure 17.5% of actives carry a price reduction — a share that is itself falling. That is their definition — a different animal from the cut ledger in the Tape, which counts events. Both clocks are right. A market can warm against last summer and still be stressed against the before-times. Southwest Florida is doing both at once, and any story that quotes one clock without naming its baseline is selling you a time zone.

The Atlas

Seven cities, fourteen communities, one yardstick.

Nobody publishes the market at this grain, so we did: inside each city, the priciest community held against the cheapest, both measured the same way — median assessed “just value” on the counties' own parcel rolls (Florida DOR, as of 07/20/2026). Communities of roughly 50–2,000 homes; ratios computed in code, not estimated. The finding arrives before the table does: the gap itself bifurcates.

Naples

241.6x

City baseline · listing median $699,900 · rent $5,500/mo · Realtor.com, June 2026

Ft Charles Dr Sect, Port Royal — 58 homes, median $15,127,191 · vs · Holiday Manor Cooperative — 249 homes, a 1975 mobile-home co-op, median $62,610.

Two hundred forty-one times, inside one city's limits — the widest split we measured anywhere.

Bonita Springs

113.7x

Marco Island

15.4x

Madeira — 100 homes, median $3,548,925, 2006 · vs · Ville de Marco — 91 homes, median $231,160, 1970.

Marco runs the region's strangest split: the hottest rent ZIP in Southwest Florida (+10.0%, June) and its third-most-stressed seller ZIP (78/100) — condo owners under assessment pressure, renting into a tourist market that never blinked.

Estero

14.7x

Corkscrew Ranch — 59 homes, median $1,311,008, built 2023 · vs · Cypress Bend RV Resort — 230 homes, median $89,471, 1989.

Lehigh Acres

4.1x

City baseline · listing median $329,000 · rent $1,850/mo · the only SWFL city with rising inventory, +3.74% YoY · Realtor.com, June 2026

Ibis Landing — 105 homes, built 2024, median $345,622 · vs · Orange Grove Pk Condo — 158 homes, 1972, median $84,465.

Even Lehigh. The community built in 2024 against the 1972 condo — and the whole spread is 4x, in the one city where supply is piling up.

Coastal cities split 15x to 242x inside their own limits; inland Lehigh splits 4x. The closer you stand to the water, the harder the market bifurcates — the same split the tiers showed at ZIP grain, running fractal at community grain. And read the ratios honestly: in every city, the entry side is structurally condos, co-ops, or mobile-home land, and the top side is single-family on water or golf. The ratio measures product mix as much as location. That isn't a flaw in the number. That is what the bottom of a market is.

The Watch

Dated. Graded next issue.

Three things with dates on them. For each: what we expect, and what would prove us wrong. Issue 002 scores all three in print.

07/31/2026 · Marco Island

The Hilton doubling gets its verdict.

Marco Island's planning board rules on the Hilton's bid to double its room count — continued from early July. We expect approval: bets on tourist capacity have been landing all year (the $1.1B RSW build, the $13M Fort Myers Beach resort start, the $41.25M Naples Bay Resort trade).

Proves us wrong: a denial, or a second continuance — either says the island's appetite for tourist capacity has a ceiling the money hasn't found yet.

Council calendar · Naples

The ground under the airport gets a price.

Naples city council and the airport authority met for the third time on 07/21/2026 over a new land lease — the proposal now includes a purchase option, after an appraisal put the lease's worth at $8M–$10.8M a year. We expect the terms to advance; nobody convenes a third meeting to renew the status quo.

Proves us wrong: talks collapse into a status-quo renewal — the appraisal becomes a museum piece.

Running · Fort Myers Beach

The island re-capitalizes in public.

Three independent signals in one month: a $13M resort construction start, state stormwater money, and a record $2,000,000 condo closing on 07/24/2026 — on an island next door to the region's heaviest flood economics ($32,610 expected annual loss per insured property in Sanibel's ZIP). We expect the island to do it again — at least one more record print or project milestone before Issue 002.

Proves us wrong: the record stands alone — no follow-through print, no milestone — and the re-capitalization story was one good week.
